_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt:
Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Working Lands & Industry' — forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture, the resource economy that defines the Cariboo and rural BC.

OUT OF SCOPE — score 0-14: geopolitical and war news with no resource-economy connection; consumer tech and gadget reviews; wildlife content with no agricultural or working-lands relevance; crime and judicial news unrelated to resource industries; financial market and stock ticker stories.

CALIBRATION — apply this ladder to everything else. Trade-press journalism counts fully: equipment, markets, and operations coverage is a real fit, not a near-zero. A BC tie raises a score but is NOT required to reach the top band.
- 80-100: Excellent working-lands journalism. BC/Cariboo forestry, ranching, mining, and agriculture stories land here (mill closures, beetle kill, BCTS, Cariboo ranchers and water rights, local mine operations, Cariboo Cattlemen) — and so does outstanding national trade reporting with real operational or economic depth.
- 55-79: Solid resource-economy journalism anywhere in Canada or beyond — Western Producer or Northern Miner-style coverage of farm machinery, harvest technology, livestock and commodity markets, mining operations and exploration, AgTech and precision agriculture, silviculture, sawmills, drone survey work, mine automation, and labour/workforce stories in these industries. Most genuine trade journalism belongs HERE, not below.
- 30-54: Broader agriculture, forestry, or mining news with clear working-lands relevance but thin reporting — general farm economics, international resource-industry briefs, climate impacts on working lands.
- 15-29: Tangential mentions — a business, policy, or science story that touches forestry/agriculture/mining in passing, or Cariboo civic news unrelated to working lands.

ANCHORS: 'Williams Lake sawmill cuts second shift as beetle-kill supply dwindles' → 95. 'New John Deere baler cuts hay-drying time by a third' → 70. 'Cattle futures slip on weaker export demand' → 60. 'Global copper prices hit two-year high' → 40.

Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items._excerpt: Incumbent Surinderpal Rathor was at home Saturday, Oct 17 where he anxiously awaited election results. Preliminary results from this year's municipal election in Williams Lake. Official results won't be declared until Wednesday, Oct. 21. Also at home Saturday, Oct. 17 was former mayor and challenger Walter Cobb where he too awaited election results. Incumbent Surinderpal Rathor will remain mayor of Williams Lake for a second term following this year’s municipal election. According to preliminary results that were shared approximately 50 minutes after voting closed 8 p.m. at Marie Sharpe Elementary School, Rathor was identified as the successful candidate against challenger and former mayor Walt Cobb. Rathor was elected mayor in 2022 after serving as a city councillor for more than 20 years. Rathor was at home with family, friends and supporters eagerly awaiting for the results to come in, shortly after which he shared a Facebook post. “Thank you for trusting me to continue serving as your mayor. To my wife, family, campaign team and this incredible community thank you for believing in me,” he wrote. “I’m honoured, grateful and ready to keep working for you. Together we can!” In 2014 and 2018 Rathor was defeated by Cobb for the top position. Preliminary results which won’t be made official until Wednesday, Oct. 21, show Rathor securing 2,116 votes (913 advance and 1,203 general) compared to Cobb’s total of 1,026 (530 advance and 496 general). Councillor incumbents Scott Nelson and Michael Moses were also successfully re-elected. New faces set to take up a councillor seat include Ruth Lloyd and Nathan Wiebe with past city councillors Jason Ryll and Paul French returning. City of Williams Lake chief election officer Ross Coupé said there were a total of 3,182 ballots cast. Preliminary results show incumbent Sheila Boehm unsuccessful in her re-election efforts. Coun. Joan Flaspohler, Jazmyn Lyons and Angie Delainey did not seek re-election.

Incumbents Debra McKelvie and Martin Runge did not receive enough votes to be re-elected, with 750 and 725 votes respectively. Newcomers Jeremy Drew and Ryan Adams also earned seats on council, receiving 1,281 and 809 votes, respectively. Drew received the highest vote total among the councillors listed. items.summary: Seven trustees have been elected or acclaimed to the School District 27 board of education, according to preliminary results from the Oct. 17 elections. items._excerpt: Seven trustees have been elected or acclaimed to the School District 27 board of education, according to preliminary results from the Oct. 17 elections. Voters have chosen their school trustees for Cariboo-Chilcotin School District 27 following the Oct. 17 election. Fourteen candidates filed nominations for the board’s seven seats. Three trustees were elected by acclamation and the remaining four seats were decided by voters. William Shepherd of 108 Mile Ranch was acclaimed in Zone 2, while incumbent Michael Franklin and Jenny Philbrick, both of Williams Lake, were acclaimed in zones 6 and 7, respectively. Michael Henshall, representing 100 Mile House, won Zone 3 with 345 votes receiving 60.3 per cent of the vote over current board member Camille Macdonald of 70 Mile House. Mary Forbes of Williams Lake, a longtime trustee and the board’s current vice-chair, was re-elected for Zone 5 with 280 votes receiving 64.1 per cent of the vote. For Zone 1, Ella Brown (Elizabeth) got elected with 230 votes receiving 30.8 per cent of the vote, while incumbant Melissa Coates, who joined the board after winning a local by-election in June 2025 was re-elected for Zone 4 with 83 votes receiving 79.8 per cent of the vote. A total of 1,860 ballots were cast across the district in the school trustee election. These results are preliminary and subject to confirmation by the chief election officer. Official results must be declared by 4 p.m. on Wednesday, Oct. 21.
